issues.legal_issue: Repeal of a provision that transferred a pending suit to a specialist tribunal does not remove that tribunal’s jurisdiction over the suit where the transfer was lawful and no contrary legislative intention appears.
material_facts: A suit was lawfully transferred to the specialist tribunal under a statutory provision while the suit was pending.
The provision authorizing the transfer was later repealed while the suit remained pending before the tribunal.
The amending legislation contained no indication of a contrary intention.
issues.conclusion: The repeal did not affect the pending proceeding, and the tribunal retained jurisdiction to continue hearing the suit.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 8 of the Bengal General Clauses Act, 1899, repeal does not affect the previous operation of the repealed enactment, a transfer lawfully made under it, or anything duly done under it, unless a contrary intention appears. The court also relied on the absence of such an intention in the amending legislation.

rule.if: transferred_suit and transfer_was_lawful and suit_pending_at_repeal and no_contrary_intention

predicates.transferred_suit: The proceeding was a suit transferred from an ordinary court to a specialist tribunal.
predicates.transfer_was_lawful: The transfer was made lawfully under the authority then in force.
predicates.suit_pending_at_repeal: The transferred suit remained pending before the tribunal when the transfer-authorizing provision was repealed.
predicates.no_contrary_intention: The amending legislation showed no intention to terminate the tribunal’s authority over pending transferred suits.

issues.definition: When a lawfully transferred suit remains pending at repeal and the amending legislation shows no contrary intention, the tribunal continues to have jurisdiction over it.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory restriction on a landlord’s right to evict a tenant does not displace a contractual requirement to give notice before seeking possession.
material_facts: The proceeding was a landlord’s suit to evict a tenant under a rent-protection law.
The lease required the landlord to give the tenant six months’ notice before requiring the tenant to vacate, including where the lease was not renewed.
The landlord sought eviction on grounds provided by the rent-protection law, but did not give the required notice.
The tenant relied on the lease’s notice requirement.
issues.conclusion: The statutory eviction grounds did not excuse compliance with the lease’s notice requirement, and the eviction suit could not succeed because the required notice had not been given.
issues.legal_principle: The court construed section 3 of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949, as imposing additional restrictions on eviction rather than granting landlords new rights or displacing contractual rights. Its non-obstante clause means that a landlord otherwise entitled to possession must still establish a statutory ground for eviction; it does not eliminate a contractual notice requirement. The court relied on Meghji Lakshamshi and Bros. v. Furniture Workshop, Abasbhai v. Gulamnabi, Mangilal v. Sugan Chand, Haji Mohammad v. Rebati Bhushan, and Monmatha Nath v. Banarasi, and considered the contrary view in R. Krishnamurthy v. Parthasarathy incorrect. It also referred to section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, in explaining the general requirement to terminate a contractual tenancy before seeking possession.

predicates.eviction_suit_under_rent_protection_law: A landlord brought a proceeding to evict a tenant under a rent-protection law.
predicates.lease_requires_notice: The lease required the landlord to give notice before requiring the tenant to vacate.
predicates.required_notice_not_given: The landlord did not give the notice required by the lease before seeking eviction.

issues.definition: If a landlord seeks eviction under a rent-protection law, the lease requires notice, and the landlord has not given it, the eviction claim cannot succeed.
